title: حِكَايَةُ الْمَلِكِ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ
part: Night 82 · King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 474–475 (Night 82, continuing directly from nights-81), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 82 continues the tale of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān. The fourth slave-girl’s stories of the pious end with Bishr the Barefoot’s sister, the pilgrim Manṣūr ibn ʿAmmār and the man who died on hearing a verse; then the fifth slave-girl takes up the sayings of the righteous forebears and the story of Moses at the well of Midian, until dawn cuts Shahrazād off. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الثَّانِيَةُ وَالثَّمَانُونَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-thāniyatu wa-al-thamānūna
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the second and the eighty,
sentences.i: And when it was the eighty-second night,

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدَأَنَّ الْوَزِيرَ دَنْدَانَ قَالَ لِضَوْءِ الْمَكَانِ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīda anna al-wazīra dandāna qāla li-ḍawʾi al-makāni
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O king the happy, that the vizier Dandān said to Ḍawʾ al-Makān:
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the vizier Dandān said to Ḍawʾ al-Makān:
sentences.n: The print runs أن into the word before it (السعيدان, “the happy — that”); it is read as two words.

sentences.t: إِنَّ الْجَارِيَةَ قَالَتْ لِوَالِدِكَ إِنَّ أُخْتَ بِشْرٍ الْحَافِي قَصَدَتْ أَحْمَدَ بْنَ حَنْبَلٍ فَقَالَتْ لَهُ
sentences.tr: inna al-jāriyata qālat li-wālidika inna ukhta bishrin al-ḥāfī qaṣadat aḥmada bna ḥanbalin fa-qālat lahu
sentences.l: That the girl said to your father: The sister of Bishr the Barefoot made for Aḥmad son-of Ḥanbal, and she said to him:
sentences.i: The girl said to your father: The sister of Bishr the Barefoot went to Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal and said to him,
sentences.n: The Bishr meant is Bishr al-Ḥāfī, the Barefoot, an early Sufi of Baghdad (d. 227/841–2); Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, the jurist, was his contemporary. The speaker is the fourth slave-girl, whose stories Dandān is repeating to Ḍawʾ al-Makān.

sentences.t: يَا إِمَامَ الدِّينِ إِنَّا قَوْمٌ نَغْزِلُ بِاللَّيْلِ وَنَشْتَغِلُ بِمَعَاشِنَا فِي النَّهَارِ وَرُبَّمَا تَمُرُّ بِنَا مَشَاعِلُ وُلَاةِ بَغْدَادَ وَنَحْنُ عَلَى السَّطْحِ نَغْزِلُ فِي ضَوْئِهَا فَهَلْ يَحْرُمُ عَلَيْنَا ذَلِكَ
sentences.tr: yā imāma al-dīni innā qawmun naghzilu bi-al-layli wa-nashtaghilu bi-maʿāshinā fī al-nahāri wa-rubbamā tamurru binā mashāʿilu wulāti baghdāda wa-naḥnu ʿalā al-saṭḥi naghzilu fī ḍawʾihā fa-hal yaḥrumu ʿalaynā dhālika
sentences.l: O imam of the religion, we are a people who spin by night and busy-ourselves with our livelihood by day, and perhaps there pass by us the torches of the governors of Baghdad while we are on the roof spinning in their light; so is that forbidden to us?
sentences.i: “O imam of the faith, we are folk who spin by night and work at our livelihood by day. Sometimes the torches of Baghdad’s governors pass by us while we are on the roof spinning, and we spin by their light. Is that forbidden to us?”
sentences.n: معاشنا is مَعَاش, “livelihood”, with the first-person-plural suffix.

sentences.t: قَالَ لَهَا مَنْ أَنْتِ قَالَتْ أُخْتُ بِشْرٍ الْحَافِي
sentences.tr: qāla lahā man anti qālat ukhtu bishrin al-ḥāfī
sentences.l: He said to her: Who are you? She said: The sister of Bishr the Barefoot.
sentences.i: He said to her, “Who are you?” She said, “The sister of Bishr the Barefoot.”

sentences.t: فَقَالَ يَا أَهْلَ بِشْرٍ لَا أَزَالُ أَسْتَشِفُّ الْوَرَعَ مِنْ قُلُوبِكُمْ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla yā ahla bishrin lā azālu astashiffu al-wiraʿa min qulūbikum
sentences.l: And he said: O family of Bishr, I do not cease to see-through the scrupulousness from your hearts.
sentences.i: He said, “O house of Bishr, I never cease to see scrupulous piety shining out of your hearts.”
sentences.n: أستشفّ is from اِسْتَشَفَّ, “to see through” a thin thing, hence “to perceive the glow of”; the idiom here is Ibn Ḥanbal’s: he can see piety shining through them.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ بَعْضُ الْعَارِفِينَ إِذَا أَرَادَ اللَّهُ بِعَبْدٍ خَيْرًا فَتَحَ عَلَيْهِ بَابَ الْعَمَلِ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla baʿḍu al-ʿārifīna idhā arāda allāhu bi-ʿabdin khayran fataḥa ʿalayhi bāba al-ʿamali
sentences.l: And some of the knowers said: When God wills with a servant good, He opens upon him the door of work.
sentences.i: One of the gnostics said, “When God wills good for a servant, He opens to him the door of good works.”
sentences.n: العارفون, “the knowers”, is the Sufi term for those who have direct knowledge (maʿrifa) of God.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ مَالِكُ ابْنُ دِينَارٍ إِذَا مَرَّ فِى السُّوقِ وَرَأَى مَا يَشْتَهِيهِ يَقُولُ يَا نَفْسُ صَابِرِي فَلَا أُوَافِقُكِ عَلَى مَا تُرِيدِينَ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna mālikun ibnu dīnārin idhā marra fī al-sūqi wa-raʾā mā yashtahīhi yaqūlu yā nafsu ṣābirī fa-lā uwāfiquki ʿalā mā turīdīna
sentences.l: And Mālik ibn Dīnār, when he passed in the market and saw what he desired, used to say: O soul, endure! For I will not agree with you to what you want.
sentences.i: When Mālik ibn Dīnār passed through the market and saw something he desired, he would say, “O soul, be patient! I will not give in to what you want.”
sentences.n: The print writes the name as مالك ابن دينار, with ابن in the nominative, so it is read as it stands; the print’s ى in فى, بمعصيتى and منى is its usual spelling. Mālik ibn Dīnār (d. c. 130/748) was a famous Basran ascetic.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ رَضِىَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ سَلَامَةُ النَّفْسِ فِي مُخَالَفَتِهَا وَبَلَاؤُهَا فِي مُتَابَعَتِهَا
sentences.tr: wa-qāla raḍiya allāhu ʿanhu salāmatu al-nafsi fī mukhālafatihā wa-balāʾuhā fī mutābaʿatihā
sentences.l: And he said, God be pleased with him: The safety of the soul is in opposing it, and its affliction is in following it.
sentences.i: He said, God be pleased with him, “The soul’s safety lies in opposing it, and its affliction in following it.”
sentences.n: The print spells رضى with a final ى.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ مَنْصُورُ بْنُ عَمَّارٍ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla manṣūru bnu ʿammārin
sentences.l: And Manṣūr son-of ʿAmmār said:
sentences.i: Manṣūr ibn ʿAmmār said,

sentences.t: حَجَجْتُ حَجَّةً فَقَصَدْتُ مَكَّةَ مِنْ طَرِيقِ الْكُوفَةِ وَكَانَتْ لَيْلَةً مُظْلِمَةً وَإِذَا بِصَارِخٍ يَصْرُخُ فِي جَوْفِ اللَّيْلِ وَيَقُولُ
sentences.tr: ḥajajtu ḥajjatan fa-qaṣadtu makkata min ṭarīqi al-kūfati wa-kānat laylatan muẓlimatan wa-idhā bi-ṣārikhin yaṣrukhu fī jawfi al-layli wa-yaqūlu
sentences.l: I made-the-pilgrimage a pilgrimage and made for Mecca by the road of Kūfa, and it was a dark night, and behold, a crier crying in the belly of the night, and saying:
sentences.i: I made a pilgrimage, taking the road to Mecca by way of Kūfa. It was a dark night, and suddenly a man cried out in the depths of it, saying,
sentences.n: وَإِذَا بِصَارِخٍ: the بِـ after إذا of surprise only marks what appears, “and behold, a crier”. Manṣūr ibn ʿAmmār (d. c. 225/840) was a celebrated preacher of Baghdad.

sentences.t: إِلَهِي وَعِزَّتِكَ وَجَلَالِكَ مَا أَرَدْتُ بِمَعْصِيَتِى مُخَالَفَتَكَ وَمَا أَنَا جَاهِلٌ بِكَ وَلَكِنْ خَطِيئَةٌ قَضَيْتَهَا عَلَيَّ فِي قَدِيمِ أَزَلِكَ فَاغْفِرْلِي مَا فَرَطَ مِنِّى فَإِنِّي قَدْ عَصَيْتُكَ بِجَهْلِي
sentences.tr: ilāhī wa-ʿizzatika wa-jalālika mā aradtu bi-maʿṣiyatī mukhālafataka wa-mā anā jāhilun bika wa-lākin khaṭīʾatun qaḍaytahā ʿalayya fī qadīmi azalika fa-ighfir-lī mā faraṭa minnī fa-innī qad ʿaṣaytuka bi-jahlī
sentences.l: My God, by-your-might and your majesty, I did not intend by my disobedience opposition-to-You, nor am I ignorant of You; but a sin You decreed upon me in the ancient of Your eternity; so forgive me what has passed from me, for I have disobeyed You in my ignorance.
sentences.i: “My God, by Your might and Your majesty, I did not mean by my disobedience to oppose You, nor am I ignorant of You. It was a sin You had decreed for me in Your ancient eternity. Forgive me what has slipped from me, for I disobeyed You only through ignorance.”
sentences.n: The print joins فاغفر and لي into one word, فاغفرلي (“so-forgive-for-me”); it is kept as one word and read as فَاغْفِرْ لِي. The و of وعزتك is the oath particle “by”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا فَرَغَ مِنْ دُعَائِهِ تَلَا هَذِهِ الْآيَةَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā faragha min duʿāʾihi talā hādhihi al-āyata
sentences.l: And when he finished his supplication he recited this verse:
sentences.i: When he had finished his prayer he recited this verse:

sentences.t: يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا قُوْا أَنْفُسَكُمْ وَأَهْلِيكُمْ نَارًا وَقُودُهَا النَّاسُ وَالْحِجَارَةُ
sentences.tr: yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū qū anfusakum wa-ahlīkum nāran waqūduhā al-nāsu wa-al-ḥijāratu
sentences.l: O you who have believed, protect your selves and your families from a fire whose fuel is the people and the stones.
sentences.i: “O you who believe, guard yourselves and your families against a fire whose fuel is people and stones.”
sentences.n: Qurʾān 66:6. The print marks قُوْا, and the mark is kept.

sentences.t: فَسَمِعْتُ سَقْطَةً لَمْ أَعْرِفْ لَهَا حَقِيقَةً فَمَضَيْتُ
sentences.tr: fa-samiʿtu saqṭatan lam aʿrif lahā ḥaqīqatan fa-maḍaytu
sentences.l: And I heard a fall, I did not know a reality for it, and I went on.
sentences.i: Then I heard a thud, the cause of which I could not tell, and I went on my way.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَ الْغَدُ مَشَيْنَا إِلَى مَدْرَجِنَا وَإِذَا بِجِنَازَةٍ خَرَجَتْ وَوَرَاءَهَا عَجُوزٌ ذَهَبَتْ قُوَّتُهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kāna al-ghadu mashaynā ilā madrajinā wa-idhā bi-janāzatin kharajat wa-warāʾahā ʿajūzun dhahabat quwwatuhā
sentences.l: And when it was the morrow we walked to our path, and behold, a funeral had come out, and behind it an old woman, her strength gone.
sentences.i: The next morning we walked on along our road, and there a funeral procession came out with an old woman behind it, her strength spent.
sentences.n: مدرجنا is “our route”, the path of the caravan.

sentences.t: فَسَأَلْتُهَا عَنِ الْمَيِّتِ فَقَالَتْ هَذِهِ جَنَازَةُ رَجُلٍ كَانَ مَرَّبِنَا الْبَارِحَةَ وَوَلَدِي قَائِمٌ يُصَلِّي فَتَلَا آيَةً مِنْ كِتَابِ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى فَانْفَطَرَتْ مَرَارَةُ ذَلِكَ الرَّجُلِ فَوَقَعَ مَيِّتًا
sentences.tr: fa-saʾaltuhā ʿani al-mayyiti fa-qālat hādhihi janāzatu rajulin kāna marra binā al-bāriḥata wa-waladī qāʾimun yuṣallī fa-talā āyatan min kitābi allāhi taʿālā fa-infaṭarat marāratu dhālika al-rajuli fa-waqaʿa mayyitan
sentences.l: And I asked her about the dead one, and she said: This is the funeral of a man who passed by us last night, and my son was standing praying, and he recited a verse from the Book of God, exalted, and the gall-bladder of that man burst, and he fell dead.
sentences.i: I asked her about the dead man. She said, “This is the funeral of a man who passed by us last night. My son was standing in prayer and recited a verse from the Book of God Most High, and the man’s gall-bladder burst and he fell dead.”
sentences.n: The print runs كان مر بنا together as كان مرّبنا (“who passed by us”) and marks the shadda; it is read as two words. مرارة means both “bitterness” and “gall-bladder”: the old idiom has the heart’s bile burst from fear.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ تَأَخَّرَتِ الْجَارِيَةُ الرَّابِعَةُ وَتَقَدَّمَتِ الْجَارِيَةُ الْخَامِسَةُ وَقَالَتْ
sentences.tr: thumma taʾakhkharati al-jāriyatu al-rābiʿatu wa-taqaddamati al-jāriyatu al-khāmisatu wa-qālat
sentences.l: Then the fourth girl drew back and the fifth girl came forward and said:
sentences.i: Then the fourth girl stepped back and the fifth came forward and said,

sentences.t: وَهَا أَنَا أَذْكُرُ بَعْضَ مَا يَحْضُرُنِي مِنْ أَخْبَارِ السَّلَفِ الصَّالِحِ
sentences.tr: wa-hā anā adhkuru baʿḍa mā yaḥḍuruni min akhbāri al-salafi al-ṣāliḥi
sentences.l: And here I am, I mention some of what is present to me of the reports of the righteous forebears.
sentences.i: “Here I shall tell some of what comes to my mind of the accounts of the righteous forebears.”

sentences.t: كَانَ مَسْلَمَةُ بْنُ دِينَارٍ يَقُولُ عِنْدَ تَصْحِيحِ الضَّمَائِرِ تُغْفَرُ الصَّغَائِرُ وَالْكَبَائِرُ وَإِذَا عَزَمَ الْعَبْدُ عَلَى تَرْكِ الْآثَامِ أَتَاهُ الْفُتُوحُ
sentences.tr: kāna maslamatu bnu dīnārin yaqūlu ʿinda taṣḥīḥi al-ḍamāʾiri tughfaru al-ṣaghāʾiru wa-al-kabāʾiru wa-idhā ʿazama al-ʿabdu ʿalā tarki al-āthāmi atāhu al-futūḥu
sentences.l: Maslama son-of Dīnār used to say: At the correcting of the consciences, the small sins and the great are forgiven; and when the servant resolves upon leaving the sins, openings come to him.
sentences.i: Maslama ibn Dīnār used to say, “When the conscience is set right, sins small and great are forgiven; and when a servant resolves to give up sins, openings come to him.”
sentences.n: الفتوح (“openings”) is the Sufi word for the gifts of insight and ease that God opens to the devoted.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ كُلُّ نِعْمَةٍ لَا تُقَرِّبُ إِلَى اللَّهِ فَهِيَ بَلِيَّةٌ وَقَلِيلُ الدُّنْيَا يَشْغَلُ عَنْ كَثِيرِ الْآخِرَةِ وَكَثِيرُهَا يُنْسِيكَ قَلِيلَهَا
sentences.tr: wa-qāla kullu niʿmatin lā tuqarribu ilā allāhi fa-hiya baliyyatun wa-qalīlu al-dunyā yashghalu ʿan kathīri al-ākhirati wa-kathīruhā yunsīka qalīlahā
sentences.l: And he said: Every blessing that does not bring-near to God is a trial; and a little of this world occupies from much of the hereafter, and much of it makes you forget a little of it.
sentences.i: He said, “Every blessing that does not bring you nearer to God is a trial. A little of this world distracts from much of the next, and much of this world makes you forget the little of it.”
sentences.n: The last clause is as printed: “much of it makes you forget a little of it”, that is, abundance of the world makes even a small portion of the hereafter slip your mind.

sentences.t: وَسُئِلَ أَبُو حَازِمٍ مَنْ أَبْسَرُ النَّاسِ فَقَالَ رَجُلٌ أَذْهَبَ عُمْرَهُ فِي طَاعَةِ اللَّهِ
sentences.tr: wa-suʾila abū ḥāzimin man absaru al-nāsi fa-qāla rajulun adhhaba ʿumrahu fī ṭāʿati allāhi
sentences.l: And Abū Ḥāzim was asked: Who is the most abṣar of people? And he said: A man who spent his life in obedience to God.
sentences.i: Abū Ḥāzim was asked, “Who is the most fortunate of people?” He said, “A man who has spent his life in obedience to God.”
sentences.n: The print has أبسر, which is not a known superlative; the likeliest reading is أَيْسَر (“easiest, best-off”) with the letters shifted, but this is a guess, so the print is kept and read as “most fortunate” by the sense of the answer. Abū Ḥāzim is Salama ibn Dīnār, a Medinan ascetic of the 2nd century.

sentences.t: قَالَ فَمَنْ أَحْمَقُ النَّاسِ قَالَ رَجُلٌ بَاعَ آخِرَتَهُ بِدُنْيَا غَيْرِهِ
sentences.tr: qāla fa-man aḥmaqu al-nāsi qāla rajulun bāʿa ākhiratahu bi-dunyā ghayrihi
sentences.l: He said: Then who is the most foolish of people? He said: A man who sold his hereafter for another’s world.
sentences.i: He said, “And who is the most foolish of people?” He said, “A man who sells his hereafter for someone else’s worldly goods.”

sentences.t: وَرُوِيَ أَنَّ مُوسَى عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ لَمَّا وَرَدَمَاءَ مَدْيَنَ قَالَ
sentences.tr: wa-ruwiya anna mūsā ʿalayhi al-salāmu lammā warada māʾa madyana qāla
sentences.l: And it is related that Moses, peace be upon him, when he came to the water of Midian, said:
sentences.i: It is told that when Moses, peace be upon him, came to the water of Midian he said,
sentences.n: The print runs the verb and its object together (وردماء); they are read as two words. The story follows Qurʾān 28:23–28.

sentences.t: رَبِّ إِنِّي لِمَا أَنْزَلْتَ إِلَيَّ مِنْ خَيْرٍ فَقِيرٌ
sentences.tr: rabbi innī li-mā anzalta ilayya min khayrin faqīrun
sentences.l: My Lord, I am, for what You have sent down to me of good, needy.
sentences.i: “My Lord, I am in need of whatever good You send down to me.”
sentences.n: Qurʾān 28:24. The print marks this verse; its kasra stands over the ر instead of the ب, which is a slip, and the pointing is regularised to رَبِّ. لِمَا is the لِـ of need: “in need for what …”.

sentences.t: فَسَأَلَ مُوسَى رَبَّهُ وَلَمْ يَسْأَلِ النَّاسَ
sentences.tr: fa-saʾala mūsā rabbahu wa-lam yasʾali al-nāsa
sentences.l: So Moses asked his Lord and did not ask the people.
sentences.i: So Moses asked his Lord, and did not ask people.

sentences.t: وَجَاءَتِ الْجَارِيَتَانِ فَسَقَى لَهُمَا وَلَمْ تُصْدِرِ الرِّعَاءُ فَلَمَّا رَجَعَتَا أَخْبَرَتَا أَبَا هُمَا شُعَيْبًا عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ فَقَالَ لَعَلَّهُ جَائِعٌ
sentences.tr: wa-jāʾati al-jāriyatāni fa-saqā lahumā wa-lam tuṣdiri al-riʿāʾu fa-lammā rajaʿatā akhbaratā abāhumā shuʿayban ʿalayhi al-salāmu fa-qāla laʿallahu jāʾiʿun
sentences.l: And the two girls came, and he watered for them, and the shepherds did not send-back their flocks; and when the two returned they informed their father Shuʿayb, peace be upon him, and he said: Perhaps he is hungry.
sentences.i: The two girls came, and he watered their flock, though the shepherds had not yet driven theirs away. When the two returned they told their father, Shuʿayb, peace be upon him, and he said, “Perhaps he is hungry.”
sentences.n: The print writes ابا هما with a space (“father of-them”); it is kept as printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَ لِأَحْدِيهِمَا ارْجِعِي إِلَيْهِ وَادْعِيهِ
sentences.tr: thumma qāla li-aḥdīhimā irjiʿī ilayhi wa-adʿīhi
sentences.l: Then he said to one-of-the-two: Go back to him and call him.
sentences.i: Then he said to one of them, “Go back to him and call him.”
sentences.n: The print has لاحديهما for لإحداهما (“to one of the two”), a spelling of the ʿāmmiyya kind; it is kept as printed.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَتَتْهُ غَطَّتْ وَجْهَهَا وَقَالَتْ إِنَّ أَبِي يَدْعُوكَ لِيَجْزِيَكَ أَجْرَ مَاسَقَيْتَ لَنَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā atathu gharṭat wajhahā wa-qālat inna abī yadʿūka li-yajziyaka ajra mā saqayta lanā
sentences.l: And when she came to him she covered her face and said: My father calls you that he may recompense you the wage of what you watered for us.
sentences.i: When she came to him she covered her face and said, “My father calls you so that he may pay you the wage for watering for us.”
sentences.n: The print runs أجر ما سقيت together as اجر ماسقيت; it is read as three words.

sentences.t: فَكَرِهَ مُوسَى ذَلِكَ وَأَرَادَأَنْ لَايَتْبَعَهَا
sentences.tr: fa-kariha mūsā dhālika wa-arāda an lā yatbaʿahā
sentences.l: And Moses disliked that, and wished that he not follow her.
sentences.i: Moses disliked this, and wished not to walk behind her.
sentences.n: The print runs وأراد أن لا together as وارادان لايتبعها, with أن and لا joined to their neighbours; read as separate words.

sentences.t: وَكَانَتِ امْرَأَةً ذَاتَ عَجُزٍ فَكَانَتِ الرِّيحُ تَضْرِبُ ثَوْبَهَا فَيَظْهَرُ لِمُوسَى عَجُزُهَا فَيَغُضُّ بَصَرَهُ
sentences.tr: wa-kānati imraʾatan dhāta ʿajuzin fa-kānati al-rīḥu taḍribu thawbahā fa-yaẓharu li-mūsā ʿajuzuhā fa-yaghuḍḍu baṣarahu
sentences.l: And she was a woman possessed of hips, and the wind would strike her garment, and her hips would appear to Moses, and he would lower his gaze.
sentences.i: She was a woman of ample hips, and the wind would blow against her garment so that her hips showed to Moses, and he would lower his eyes.
sentences.n: عَجُز is the hindquarters, here the hips and buttocks; the Arabic is frank, and so is the translation.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَ لَهَا كُونِي خَلْفِي وَأَنَا أَمَامَكِ فَمَشَتْ خَلْفَهُ حَتَّى دَخَلَ عَلَى شُعَيْبٍ عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ وَالْعَشَاءُ مُهَيَّءٌ
sentences.tr: thumma qāla lahā kūnī khalfī wa-anā amāmaki fa-mashat khalfahu ḥattā dakhala ʿalā shuʿaybin ʿalayhi al-salāmu wa-al-ʿashāʾu muhayyaʾun
sentences.l: Then he said to her: Be behind me, and I am in front of you; so she walked behind him until he entered upon Shuʿayb, peace be upon him, and the supper was prepared.
sentences.i: Then he said to her, “Walk behind me while I walk ahead of you.” She walked behind him until he came in to Shuʿayb, peace be upon him, and supper was ready.
sentences.n: The print spells the participle مهيء; it is read as مُهَيَّأ, “made ready”.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَ زَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: Morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent, leaving the permitted speech.
sentences.n: The closing formula, with its rhyme on -āḥ, as in every night.
